newsitem.title: INDIA: India rulers link 1997/98 budget to survival.
newsitem.headline: India rulers link 1997/98 budget to survival.

text.p: India's embattled ruling coalition said on Wednesday that the fate of its path-breaking 1997/98 (April-March) budget depended on the survival of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front government.
"It depends on the survival of the government," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy told Reuters.
Reddy had been asked if the chances of parliament approving the budget had brightened following the prospect of formal talks between the United Front coalition and the Congress party.
"Naturally so," Reddy said when asked if the fate of the budget was linked to the survival of the government.
The nation's main Bombay share index on Wednesday jumped 100.20 points, or 2.85 percent, to 3,620.69 points minutes after opening on news of formal talks between the United Front and Congress.
The ruling United Front coalition had said it would begin formal talks with the Congress party on Wednesday, raising hopes of a solution to the country's political crisis.
The budget, now before parliament, has been held hostage to the political crisis.
The budget was called into question after the Congress withdrew its support to Deve Gowda on March 30, triggering a political crisis that jolted the financial markets.
President Shankar Dayal Sharma has asked Deve Gowda to face a confidence vote in parliament on April 11.
Deve Gowda's centre-left minority coalition has been in power for 10 months, relying on the support of 138 Congress lawmakers to survive in parliament.
Industry and trade bodies have urged parliament to approve the budget, which radically lowered income tax, slashed corporate tax and reduced import tariffs.
"We are not only hopeful but confident that the budget will be passed," H.S. Tandon, secretary general of the Punjab, Haryana, Delhi Chambers of Commerce and Industry, told Reuters.
Most parties have agreed not to allow the political crisis to derail the budget, which was presented by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on February 28.
But they have offered different solutions to end the impasse, including a proposal to take up the discussion on the budget after the vote of confidence.
The speaker of parliament, P.A. Sangma, told reporters last week that there were constitutional precedents that the budget could be approved by parliament after the confidence vote.
